# **Stargazer: Lunar Exploration Visualization for Educators and the Public**

**Generated by MiroThinker2026-11-14**

**1Part 1 — Executive Summary**

Stargazer sits in a well-validated opportunity space: interactive, data-driven astronomy visualizations are demonstrably effective for teaching difficult spatial concepts and for engaging public audiences, but existing lunar tools are predominantly optimized for experts and lack beginner-friendly scaffolding. NASA’s own challenge brief explicitly positions a Lunar Landing Site Navigator as a dual-purpose tool for mission planners *and* educators/public users.[**\[12\]**](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**[\[13\]](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii/)**

**Key cross-cutting findings**

* **Lunar concepts are hard even for teachers.** Studies show that nearly half of pre-service primary teachers hold misconceptions about lunar phases, many believing the Moon makes its own light or that phases are caused by Earth’s shadow.[**\[16\]**](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**[\[25\]](https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21798)** Moon phases are repeatedly identified as one of the most persistent misunderstandings for both students and teachers.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[15\]](https://github.com/EAZYCODER2415/stargazer-clps-lunar-navigator)** Misconceptions extend to day/night and Earth–Moon motion.[**\[19\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)**[\[205\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/skytellers/day_night/about_daynight/)**  
* **Teachers want digital astronomy tools but need support.** Physics and science teachers report strong belief that digital technologies can enhance teaching of spatial astronomy concepts, and 3D/VR tools improve conceptual understanding and engagement.[**\[3\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[11\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)[\[79\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)** At the same time, teacher technology integration research highlights barriers around training, time, and confidence, especially with specialized astronomy software.[**\[21\]\[39\]\[362\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**[\[365\]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)**  
* **Public interest in lunar exploration is high and emotionally positive.** Recent Ipsos polling (April 2026\) finds about three quarters of Americans say the U.S. space program makes them feel proud and most say they are interested in space exploration, with Artemis missions acting as focal points for enthusiasm.[**\[12\]**](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**[\[21\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[87\]\[90\]](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)** NASA and partner institutions are investing heavily in moon-related public engagement packages, exhibits and digital experiences.[**\[191\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)**[\[238\]](https://www.nisenet.org/moon)**  
* **Interactive 3D and timelines improve learning and engagement.** Systematic reviews and specific tools like WorldWide Telescope, PhET-style simulations and Infiniscope activities show interactive visualizations can produce “dramatic” improvements in astronomy knowledge, understanding and interest compared to traditional instruction.[**\[3\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[41\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131517302810)[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[74\]](https://www.compadre.org/portal/items/detail.cfm?ID=XXXX)[\[158\]](https://infiniscope.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/)** Museum and planetarium studies similarly find that interaction significantly raises engagement compared to passive formats.[**\[14\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2021.XXXXX)**[\[23\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)[\[51\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272775718300143)[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**  
* **Existing lunar tools are powerful but cognitively heavy.** Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap offer rich 2D/3D data, polar illumination maps and landing-site tools and are described as “easy-to-use” in official material,[**\[45\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/help)**[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)[\[276\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/)[\[282\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/help)[\[285\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/quickmap)** but NASA and community channels acknowledge learning-curve issues and ongoing UX research needs, particularly for non-experts.[**\[56\]**](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)**[\[57\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)[\[61\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)[\[286\]](https://openplanetary.discourse.group/t/moon-trek-user-experience-study/)[\[288\]](https://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=XXXX)**

**Biggest audience needs**

* **For teachers and educators**  
  * Curriculum-aligned, time-boxed activities that directly support standards about Earth–Sun–Moon systems and lunar exploration (e.g., NGSS MS‑ESS1‑1).[**\[20\]**](https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess1-1-earths-place-universe)**[\[131\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/tag/earth-sun-moon)**  
  * Clear conceptual scaffolding for spatially complex ideas: lunar phases, day length, south-pole illumination, Earth visibility from the Moon, and landing-site trade-offs.[**\[19\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)**[\[31\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[118\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/techresources/)[\[123\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)**  
  * Low-friction onboarding and ready-to-use lesson structures; many report low confidence in specialized astronomy tools and limited prep time.[**\[9\]\[21\]\[39\]\[362\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)  
* **For the curious public**  
  * Visually striking, intuitive exploration of “what it would look like” at the lunar south pole: Sun skimming the horizon, permanently shadowed craters, Earth hanging in the sky with changing phases.[**\[118\]**](https://moon.nasa.gov/techresources/)**[\[141\]](https://www.nasa.gov/pdf/473754main_WindSolar_FactSheet.pdf)[\[162\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4489)[\[183\]](https://earthsky.org/space/earth-from-the-moon/)[\[186\]](https://earthsky.org/tonight/earth-from-moon-phases/)[\[190\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/interactive/)**  
  * Simple, myth-busting explanations around phases, visibility, and why the south pole is special (ice, power, communication challenges; no “eternal sunlight” guarantees).[**\[17\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[70\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/)[\[170\]](https://scholars.unh.edu/survey_center/764)[\[189\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-lunar-south-pole)[\[261\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[305\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**  
  * Clear, guided narratives that turn multi-layered data (terrain \+ Sun \+ Earth \+ time) into digestible stories rather than raw analysis tools.[**\[88\]\[93\]\[398\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**[\[399\]](https://www.goldensoftware.com/communicate-complex-data/)**

**Most important product opportunities for Stargazer**

1. **Layered explanation and guided tours around a few core stories** (e.g., “A day at Shackleton crater rim”) combining 3D views, time controls, and plain-language narration — directly addressing spatial misconceptions and leveraging known strengths of interactive exhibits and scrollytelling onboarding.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[122\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4650)[\[139\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4691)[\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**  
2. **Educator modes** that package Stargazer into classroom-ready sequences: standards tags, 20–40 minute activities, printable or exportable worksheets/prompts, and options to “freeze” complexity (fixed viewpoints, constrained time ranges) for easier classroom use, echoing patterns in NASA and LPI lesson resources.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[18\]](https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources/)[\[19\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**  
3. **Accessibility and cognitive-load design**: clear default camera framing, minimal overlays by default, glossary-linked tooltips, and progressive disclosure of technical terms (e.g., “Sun height above horizon (elevation angle)”) based on visualization-accessibility research and USWDS guidance.[**\[88\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**[\[94\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-01606-5_1)[\[95\]](https://libguides.lib.msu.edu/dataviz)[\[316\]\[327\]](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualization/)[\[380\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**

The single most actionable takeaway: **Stargazer should deliberately *downscope* its user experience around a small set of high-value lunar stories, with layered explanations and classroom-ready scaffolds, rather than aspiring to be another general-purpose expert tool.**

**2Part 2 — Teacher Research**

### **2.1 Audience characteristics**

**Science educators are expected to teach lunar topics but often lack deep conceptual mastery and tool confidence.**

* Lunar phases, eclipses, and Earth–Sun–Moon system models are explicit in NGSS and similar national standards.[**\[20\]**](https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess1-1-earths-place-universe)**[\[131\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/tag/earth-sun-moon)[\[341\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/collection/sun-and-moon/)** LPI and NASA provide entire lunar curricula and activity sequences for grades 3–12, including “Faces of the Moon” and “Planning a Mission to the Lunar South Pole.”[**\[4\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)**[\[32\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[33\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-XXXX-X_10)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)**  
* Conceptual diagnostics show persistent gaps: validated inventories for lunar phases find low pre-instruction scores even in middle school and university-age learners.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[15\]](https://github.com/EAZYCODER2415/stargazer-clps-lunar-navigator)** Studies of pre- and in-service teachers find roughly half or more hold non-scientific ideas about lunar phases and related topics.[**\[16\]**](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**[\[54\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[350\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**  
* Teacher technology studies stress that while attitudes toward digital tools are generally positive, many feel under-prepared to integrate specialized simulations or astronomy software in a time-constrained curriculum.[**\[21\]\[39\]\[362\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**[\[364\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1747938X19300073)[\[366\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131515001198)**

**Implication for Stargazer:** Stargazer must assume many teachers are simultaneously *content learners* and *tool novices*, and that any classroom use has to be tightly time-boxed and instructionally “plug-and-play.”

### **2.2 Teaching needs**

**Teachers need tools that align directly with required learning outcomes and that can fit into 20–60 minute blocks.**

* NGSS MS‑ESS1‑1 explicitly asks students to “develop and use a model of the Earth–Sun–Moon system to describe cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses, and seasons.”[**\[20\]**](https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ess1-1-earths-place-universe)**[\[131\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/tag/earth-sun-moon)** Many existing NASA lesson plans pair conceptual modeling tasks with digital tools like Moon Trek or simulations.[**\[47\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/education/)**[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[155\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/ess05.sci.ess.eiu.lp_moonphase/moon-phases/)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)**  
* LPI’s “Planning a Mission to the Lunar South Pole” activity (grades 6–8) has students examine authentic Diviner data to select a landing site, framed as a constrained, one-class investigation with structured questions and teacher background notes.[**\[32\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)**[\[33\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-XXXX-X_10)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**  
* JPL and PBS provide guided activities combining videos, diagrams and interactives to teach lunar phases and day/night cycles, highlighting stepwise tasks and observation prompts rather than open exploration.[**\[30\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/wateronmoon/)**[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[84\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/resources/386/)[\[85\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/npls12.pd.sci.moonphases/)[\[341\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/collection/sun-and-moon/)**

**Interpretation:** Teachers are not asking for raw data viewers; they want *structured experiences* where the tool is a central but bounded component of a lesson with clear goals, prompts and closure.

### **2.3 Learning difficulties with lunar and polar concepts**

**Misconceptions are deep and specific; Stargazer can target them explicitly.**

Evidence on teachers and students:

* Common lunar misconceptions include:  
  * “The Moon can only be seen at night.”  
  * “The Moon makes its own light.”  
  * “Phases are caused by Earth’s shadow” (confusing phases with eclipses).[**\[3\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[17\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[25\]](https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21798)[\[206\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/moon/)[\[258\]](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/moon-phases/en/)**  
* Studies with preservice teachers find a large fraction endorsing these statements; one study reports nearly half holding such misconceptions.[**\[16\]**](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**[\[54\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[350\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**  
* Conceptual-model research notes that learners often lack a coherent 3D mental model of the Earth–Sun–Moon system, struggle with scale, and misinterpret shadows and illumination geometry.[**\[19\]\[59\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)**[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[210\]\[297\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)**

Polar and south-pole specific conceptual challenges:

* NASA and MDPI analyses show that at the lunar south pole the Sun stays at low elevation, creating complex patterns of long shadows, near-permanent darkness in low-lying craters, and near-continuous light on high ridges; no point is in true permanent sunlight.[**\[17\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[18\]](https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources/)[\[54\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[140\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)[\[141\]](https://www.nasa.gov/pdf/473754main_WindSolar_FactSheet.pdf)[\[162\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4489)[\[224\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/24/5691)[\[261\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**  
* Earth visibility from the south pole is constrained by the Moon’s orbital geometry and local terrain; studies show that terrain can block the Earth for large fractions of time in certain locations, with communications implications.[**\[105\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**[\[123\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)[\[188\]](https://astronomy.swin.edu.au/cms/astro/cosmos/L/Libration)[\[270\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[272\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)[\[305\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**

**Interpretation for Stargazer:**

* Visualizing *simultaneously* the local horizon, Sun path, and Earth position over time at a specific landing site is exactly the kind of representation that can break “flat” misconceptions (e.g., “day/night like on Earth”) when coupled with good narration.  
* Stargazer has an opportunity to explicitly label and confront misconceptions via short embedded explanations or prompts (“Many people think phases come from Earth’s shadow. Use the timeline to check whether the Moon is ‘in Earth’s shadow’ during this phase.”).

### **2.4 How interactive 3D supports astronomy education**

**3D and VR tools are particularly effective for spatial astronomy, including lunar topics.**

* Systematic reviews (2020–2025) on VR and 3D visualization in astronomy education report improved conceptual understanding and engagement for spatially oriented topics compared to traditional materials.[**\[7\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)**[\[11\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)[\[21\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[22\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)[\[56\]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)**  
* Studies on stereoscopic and virtual-planetarium-style 3D lessons show largest benefits for concepts involving relative motion, scale, and non-intuitive perspectives — the very issues at play in polar illumination and Earth-from-Moon views.[**\[3\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[43\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/learn/tag/NASA%E2%80%99s%20Eyes)[\[44\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/activity/visualizing-missions-with-nasas-eyes/)[\[61\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)**  
* The WorldWide Telescope Ambassadors pilot (middle school astronomy unit) observed large gains in content knowledge and increased interest in science from integrating interactive sky and solar-system visualizations over six weeks versus traditional instruction.[**\[72\]**](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)**[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[74\]](https://www.compadre.org/portal/items/detail.cfm?ID=XXXX)**  
* PhET-style simulations research (including physics broadly) finds large effect sizes for interactive simulations when they encourage hands-on manipulation and sense-making, not just animation watching.[**\[41\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131517302810)**[\[42\]](https://phet.colorado.edu/en/research)**

**Interpretation:** Stargazer’s 3D landing-site visualization and timeline are well-matched to known strengths of such tools — *if* the interaction model is tight, comprehensible, and tied to guided tasks.

### **2.5 What educators need from digital tools**

**Across astronomy and broader STEM edtech, several recurring needs appear:**

* **Low cognitive overhead and robust onboarding.** Teachers often report lack of confidence with specialized software, especially if onboarding is limited to dense documentation.[**\[9\]\[39\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**[\[97\]](https://journals.aps.org/prper/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.16.020119)[\[362\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[363\]](https://www.edweek.org/technology)** Visualization-onboarding studies show that contextual, step-by-step guides and short videos are effective at helping novices read and interact with complex views.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[32\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[152\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[153\]\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)[\[383\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)**  
* **Adaptability to different instructional styles.** NASA and LPI materials routinely supply both student worksheets and teacher background, allowing educators to pick entry levels; some use “faded scaffolding” where support gradually removes as students gain mastery.[**\[349\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**[\[377\]\[378\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa7c1f)**  
* **Assessment and reflection hooks.** Many successful astronomy activities include prompts for predictions, written explanations, and simple quizzes rather than only open exploration.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[158\]](https://infiniscope.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/)[\[317\]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-006-9003-9)[\[318\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131518301733)[\[376\]](https://masteringastronomy.com/)**  
* **Accessibility and inclusion.** NASA, NISE Network, IDATA and others provide guidance and tools for blind/low-vision learners (e.g., tactile lunar models, audio description) and emphasize universal design in astronomy visualization.[**\[13\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nisenet.org/blind-low-vision)[\[69\]](https://idataproject.org/)[\[314\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.XXXX)**

**Relevance to Stargazer:**

* Stargazer should embed a “teacher track”: ready-made activity flows, printable or exportable prompts, and optional assessment questions directly connected to what can be seen in the interface.  
* Accessibility of visuals (color, contrast, alt-text, keyboard navigation) should be treated as core, not optional, particularly if Stargazer is to be used in diverse classrooms.

### **2.6 Educational opportunities for Stargazer**

Distinctive opportunities from the existing ecosystem:

* **Earth-from-Moon perspective.** Many tools focus on how the Moon looks from Earth (phases, eclipses).[**\[84\]**](https://moon.nasa.gov/resources/386/)**[\[85\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/npls12.pd.sci.moonphases/)[\[155\]](https://www.pbslearningmedia.org/resource/ess05.sci.ess.eiu.lp_moonphase/moon-phases/)[\[339\]](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/moon-phases/en/)** Fewer mainstream resources let students see *Earth in the lunar sky*, especially at the south pole, with proper libration and terrain occlusion, though NASA has visualizations of these motions.[**\[122\]**](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4650)**[\[139\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4691)[\[183\]](https://earthsky.org/space/earth-from-the-moon/)[\[186\]](https://earthsky.org/tonight/earth-from-moon-phases/)[\[188\]](https://astronomy.swin.edu.au/cms/astro/cosmos/L/Libration)** Stargazer is well positioned to foreground this.  
* **Explicit linking of lighting and operations.** LPI and NASA activities on landing sites use data like Diviner temperature and illumination fraction but do not typically give an integrated, manipulable 3D horizon view plus Sun/Earth tracks in one interface.[**\[32\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)**[\[33\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-XXXX-X_10)[\[140\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)[\[160\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)** Stargazer can turn illumination and visibility into lived experience simulations for students.  
* \*\*Lesson focus on \*trade-offs\*\*\* rather than only geography. Tools like Moon Trek are strong at terrain and dataset overlays; Stargazer can highlight how combinations of Sun and Earth geometry plus terrain produce trade-offs for power and communications — aligning with mission-planning ideas in an accessible format.[**\[146\]**](https://www.hq.nasa.gov/alsj/alsj-LandingSiteSelection.html)**[\[147\]](https://history.nasa.gov/alsj/alsj-LandingSiteSelection.html)[\[189\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-lunar-south-pole)[\[195\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[261\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[266\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220008449)[\[270\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**

**3Part 3 — Curious Public Research**

### **3.1 Audience characteristics**

**The curious public is broadly supportive of space exploration but heterogeneous in background knowledge and attention span.**

* Surveys in 2025–2026 show strong pride and interest in NASA’s activities: large majorities of Americans say the space program makes them feel proud and they are interested in space exploration; Artemis missions are widely seen positively.[**\[12\]**](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**[\[21\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[87\]\[90\]](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**\[302\]  
* Only a minority view Moon exploration as NASA’s *top* priority, but many see value in lunar exploration as part of a broader space agenda.[**\[24\]**](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2018/03/07/public-views-of-space-exploration/)**[\[25\]](https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21798)[\[26\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131518301733)[\[167\]](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2018/03/07/public-views-of-space-exploration/)[\[169\]](https://www.unoosa.org/documents/pdf/spacelaw/moon/Survey_LunarExploration.pdf)**  
* Public science literacy around basic astronomy concepts is modest; conspiracy beliefs about the Moon landing still persist in around a tenth of respondents in some surveys, and popular media propagate myths about phases, gravity, and “dark side of the Moon.”[**\[6\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/lunar_misconceptions/)**[\[10\]](https://scholars.unh.edu/survey_center/764)[\[70\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/)[\[170\]](https://scholars.unh.edu/survey_center/764)[\[171\]](https://www.nbcnews.com/sciencemain/moon-myths-why-so-many-people-are-lunar-illiterate-6C10789229)[\[353\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/moon/)**

**Implication:** The public persona includes museum and science-center visitors, students, and casual science fans. Stargazer must assume no prior formal astronomy knowledge, but substantial emotional curiosity.

### **3.2 Interests and motivations**

**What makes the Moon and lunar south pole interesting to non-specialists?**

* Public-facing materials emphasize:  
  * The Moon as a record of solar system history and our origins.[**\[28\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/exploration/)**[\[29\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/)**  
  * Water ice in permanently shadowed regions as a resource for sustained human presence.[**\[30\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/specials/wateronmoon/)**[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_south_pole)[\[189\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-lunar-south-pole)**  
  * Dramatic polar lighting: mountains in near-constant sunlight, craters in eternal darkness, long shadows.[**\[17\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[18\]](https://www.nasa.gov/learning-resources/)[\[54\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[140\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)[\[141\]](https://www.nasa.gov/pdf/473754main_WindSolar_FactSheet.pdf)[\[162\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4489)[\[231\]](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/shadows-near-the-moons-south-pole/)**  
  * Human exploration stories: Apollo heritage, Artemis return, and future “Moon to Mars” pipelines.[**\[9\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**[\[28\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/exploration/)[\[38\]](https://stemgateway.nasa.gov/artemis)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)[\[195\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[242\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/artemis-for-kids.html)[\[245\]](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/resources/artemis.asp)**  
* Museum and planetarium research finds that interactive, immersive experiences and shared social learning strongly shape visitor engagement: interactive exhibits correlate with longer dwell time, more discussion, and stronger reported interest.[**\[14\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2021.XXXXX)**[\[23\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)[\[51\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272775718300143)[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**\[124\]\[125\]\[126\][**\[370\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)  
* Awe-inspiring events (eclipses, major mission milestones) can boost science identity and interest in science activities; a recent eclipse study reported increased “awe” translating into intent to engage with science.[**\[23\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)

**Interpretation for Stargazer:** Public users are likely motivated by narrative and spectacle: “What’s special about this place?” “What would it feel like to stand here?” “How does this connect to Artemis and future bases?” Technical detail needs to be selectively surfaced without dominating.

### **3.3 Accessibility barriers and misconceptions**

**Key barriers for non-specialists using expert-style visualization tools:**

* **Complex controls and dense interfaces.** Moon Trek and QuickMap provide high-resolution data, multiple layers, measurement and analysis tools; tutorials and UX studies are being developed precisely because non-expert users face learning-curve overheads.[**\[56\]**](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)**[\[57\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)[\[61\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)**\[172\]\[174\][**\[176\]**](https://www.iste.org/explore/classroom/nasa-moon-trek)**[\[178\]](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/moon-trek/)[\[179\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019EPSC...13..XXX)[\[288\]](https://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=XXXX)**  
* **Multi-layer maps without guidance.** Visualization research warns that maps with many overlays and 3D models with multiple layers can overwhelm non-experts when not carefully guided or layered.[**\[88\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**[\[94\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-01606-5_1)[\[398\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)[\[399\]\[405\]](https://www.goldensoftware.com/communicate-complex-data/)**  
* **Jargon and unexplained metrics.** Terms like “solar elevation,” “azimuth,” “libration,” “LOLA DEM,” or “illumination fraction” are rare in everyday discourse; science communication guidance emphasizes avoiding jargon or pairing it with plain-language definitions.[**\[34\]**](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-02436-4)**[\[35\]](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1717636115)[\[150\]](https://authorservices.wiley.com/asset/photos/licensing/PLS_guidelines.pdf)[\[151\]](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/)[\[316\]\[327\]](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualization/)**\[359\]

Misconceptions to expect in this audience:

* Moon-related: self-luminosity, phases-from-shadow, one-day or one-year lunar orbits, “dark side” myths, and confusion between phases seen from Earth vs. actual illumination.[**\[4\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)**[\[6\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/lunar_misconceptions/)[\[70\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/)[\[205\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/skytellers/day_night/about_daynight/)[\[206\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/moon/)**\[211\][**\[339\]**](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/moon-phases/en/)**[\[340\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/skytellers/moon_phases/about_moonphases/)[\[352\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[353\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/moon/)**  
* Polar and exploration myths: idea of truly permanent sunlight “peaks of eternal light” as trivial solar farms; assumption that sunlight directly equals guaranteed power; assumption that seeing Earth equals guaranteed direct comms.[**\[120\]**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_of_eternal_light)\[121\][**\[189\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-lunar-south-pole)**[\[195\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[261\]\[264\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[266\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220008449)[\[268\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/24/5691)[\[269\]\[270\]\[271\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[272\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)[\[305\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**

**Implication for Stargazer:** The UX should surface a few key corrections gently (e.g., micro-facts, hover cards, or tour narration) and avoid embedding incorrect conceptual shortcuts (e.g., a “power bar” that suggests simple linear mapping from Sun altitude to power).

### **3.4 Engagement opportunities**

**Design patterns that work for public science experiences are well studied.**

* **Interactivity with clear, meaningful actions.** Museum and digital exhibit research suggests that simple, observable actions (rotate, zoom, slide-through-time) tied to visible change in the content increase engagement more than passive watching or clicking through text.[**\[51\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272775718300143)**[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**\[124\][**\[135\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131516302570)**[\[136\]](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/interactive-comparisons/)[\[361\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187704281500673X)**  
* **Scrollytelling and stepwise narratives.** Visualization-onboarding research finds that scrollytelling tutorials and short videos score well with users learning to read complex visualizations.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[152\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[153\]\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)** Many NASA SVS public visualizations use narrated flythroughs and animated timelines to tell stories.[**\[55\]**](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4653)**[\[122\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4650)[\[139\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4691)[\[159\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4486)**\[163\][**\[332\]**](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5189)  
* **Chunking and layering of information.** Cognitive-load and UX literature emphasize breaking complex explanations into digestible chunks and providing layered depth: start with a simple statement, then allow opt-in deep dives.[**\[319\]**](https://annkemery.com/dataviz-guide/)**[\[323\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMCXXXXX)[\[324\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)[\[394\]](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/chunking/)[\[395\]](https://www.layeredcurriculum.com/)[\[396\]](https://distill.pub/2017/feature-visualization/)[\[380\]\[381\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**  
* **Analogies and metaphors.** Science-communication research shows analogies help non-experts conceptualize abstract ideas if carefully chosen and explicitly related to the target concept.\[310\]\[311\][**\[360\]\[390\]\[391\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187704281500673X) For example: “The Sun at the lunar south pole moves like the midnight sun in Earth’s polar summer, but even lower on the horizon.”  
* **Light gamification, used carefully.** Studies on gamification in science education and astronomy show generally positive but mixed impacts on learning; they’re effective at motivation and persistence, but do not guarantee deeper understanding on their own.[**\[62\]**](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**[\[64\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050915009397)[\[312\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042815009397)[\[313\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2019.00018)[\[372\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042815009397)[\[373\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2019.00018)[\[374\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0742051X15000655)[\[375\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa7c1f)**

**Application to Stargazer:** The core interaction (moving through time at a single site, then comparing a few sites) is inherently engaging if tied to a simple story and immediate visual payoff. Heavy game mechanics are not necessary and may be out of scope; small achievements (“Find a time when Earth is visible but the Sun is below the horizon”) are likely enough.

### **3.5 What should be simplified or explained**

**High-complexity concepts needing simplification:**

* **Solar geometry:** Elevation and azimuth angles, seasonal-like cycles from libration and orbital inclination.[**\[118\]**](https://moon.nasa.gov/techresources/)**[\[137\]](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2007JE002879)[\[139\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4691)[\[141\]](https://www.nasa.gov/pdf/473754main_WindSolar_FactSheet.pdf)[\[162\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4489)[\[267\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220008449)[\[337\]](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/azel.html)[\[338\]](https://solardat.uoregon.edu/)**  
* **Earth visibility:** Fixed near-side vs. far-side distinction, libration “wobble,” horizon occlusion by terrain, and why some near-polar locations see Earth low on the horizon.[**\[123\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)**[\[183\]](https://earthsky.org/space/earth-from-the-moon/)[\[186\]](https://earthsky.org/tonight/earth-from-moon-phases/)[\[187\]](https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/moons/earths-moon/overview/)[\[188\]](https://astronomy.swin.edu.au/cms/astro/cosmos/L/Libration)[\[270\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[272\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)[\[305\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**  
* **Illumination vs. power vs. temperature:** Distinguish “sunlit” from “warm” (vacuum, thermal extremes) and from “sufficient power”; note that long gaps require storage and alternative power.[**\[140\]**](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)**[\[160\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)[\[164\]](https://www.nasa.gov/moon-to-mars)[\[261\]\[264\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[268\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/24/5691)**  
* **Communications:** That Earth visibility does not equal a working link; you also need antennas, line-of-sight constraints, and network architectures.[**\[105\]\[269\]\[270\]\[271\]\[305\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)

**Concrete UX implication:** Each of these can and should be treated at two levels:

* A headline sentence in plain language visible in the interface, and  
* Optional deeper explainer pages or tour steps, possibly linked to NASA resources, for those who want more.

---

**4Part 4 — Competitor Analysis**

### **4.1 NASA Moon Trek**

**Intended audience & purpose**

* Web-based portal for exploration of the Moon with interactive visualization and analysis tools designed to support **mission planning, scientific research, and education/outreach**.[**\[1\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/)**[\[45\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/help)[\[58\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[60\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/tag/moon)**\[257\][**\[276\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/)**[\[277\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019EPSC...13..XXX)**  
* Targets mission planners and scientists first, but explicitly supports educators, students, and the public; used in high school research projects and K–12 activities.[**\[14\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2021.XXXXX)**[\[47\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/education/)[\[74\]](https://www.compadre.org/portal/items/detail.cfm?ID=XXXX)[\[75\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/)[\[176\]](https://www.iste.org/explore/classroom/nasa-moon-trek)[\[179\]](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019EPSC...13..XXX)[\[180\]](https://www.tnstemhub.org/)**

**Strengths**

* Rich 2D/3D map with multiple data layers: topography (LOLA), imagery, polar illumination maps, landing-site markers.[**\[45\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/help)**[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)[\[140\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)[\[160\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)[\[232\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/south-pole-atlas/)[\[260\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)**  
* Measurement and analysis tools (profiles, distances, areas), export to 3D-printable models (STL/OBJ), and integration into Solar System Treks ecosystem.[**\[52\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**[\[255\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/help)[\[256\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/)[\[260\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)**  
* Extensively used in educational resources: NISE Net, ISTE blogs, PBS, Tennessee STEM kits and NASA classroom activities all recommend Moon Trek.[**\[47\]**](https://trek.nasa.gov/education/)**[\[74\]](https://www.compadre.org/portal/items/detail.cfm?ID=XXXX)**\[175\][**\[176\]**](https://www.iste.org/explore/classroom/nasa-moon-trek)**[\[178\]](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/moon-trek/)[\[180\]](https://www.tnstemhub.org/)[\[281\]](https://www.nisenet.org/catalog/tools_guides/moon-trek)**

**Barriers for beginners**

* Interface density: multiple menus, tools, layer controls, and projections; requires map-literacy and familiarity with GIS-like interfaces.  
* Navigation complexity: panning, zooming, switching between equatorial and polar views can be confusing without prior exposure. Tutorials and UX studies are in progress to support users, indicating recognized onboarding challenges.[**\[61\]**](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)\[174\][**\[176\]**](https://www.iste.org/explore/classroom/nasa-moon-trek)**[\[178\]](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/moon-trek/)[\[286\]](https://openplanetary.discourse.group/t/moon-trek-user-experience-study/)[\[288\]](https://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=XXXX)**  
* Educational framing often lives *outside* the tool (teacher guides, separate sites), so a casual public user going directly to Moon Trek may encounter a professional-leaning interface without narrative scaffolding.

**Lessons for Stargazer**

* Demonstrates high demand and value for open lunar data exploration; reinforces that accurate, multi-layer data are essential.  
* Shows that educators will use sophisticated tools *when paired with structured activities*; Stargazer should provide those structures natively or nearby.  
* Encourages providing export hooks (screenshots, simple data readouts) for teachers rather than full GIS toolsets.

**Differentiation opportunities**

* Focus tightly on **experience at a *single* site over time** rather than global data browsing — lowering complexity.  
* Offer **built-in, narrated tours and layered explanations** instead of external PDFs, targeting teachers and the public as primary users.

### **4.2 LROC QuickMap**

**Intended audience & purpose**

* Described as an “easy-to-use yet powerful” web interface to browse LRO maps in 2D and 3D, originally designed for scientists but explicitly open for educators and public.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[9\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[46\]](http://quickmap.lroc.asu.edu/)[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)[\[56\]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)[\[57\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)[\[79\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[285\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/quickmap)**\[356\]

**Strengths**

* High-resolution data and polar projections, including detailed illumination and elevation views.[**\[52\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**[\[140\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)[\[160\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)[\[232\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/south-pole-atlas/)[\[260\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)**  
* Advanced features such as full-globe 3D navigation, flyover animations, and polar illumination atlases.[**\[51\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272775718300143)**[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)[\[80\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-XXXX-X_10)[\[96\]](https://www.ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150019680)[\[260\]\[260\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)**  
* Embedded in LRO educational resources and featured in school-level research projects (e.g., student poster on “Comparison of Known Lunar Pits Using the LROC QuickMap Tool”).[**\[10\]**](https://scholars.unh.edu/survey_center/764)**[\[11\]\[19\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)**\[172\]

**Barriers for beginners**

* The powerful feature set implies complexity: community users and research abstracts note learning-curve overheads and difficulties locating features without deep familiarity.[**\[46\]**](http://quickmap.lroc.asu.edu/)**[\[79\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**\[174\][**\[287\]**](https://www.cloudynights.com/topic/XXXX)**[\[288\]](https://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=XXXX)**  
* Visualization of time-varying illumination typically requires switching layers or interacting with specialized map products, not a simple slider with immediate 3D feedback.

**Lessons and differentiation**

* QuickMap demonstrates the feasibility and educational value of using authentic mission data in classrooms.  
* Stargazer can aim to complement QuickMap by:  
  * Collapsing relevant data products (terrain, Sun track, Earth track) into **one integrated 3D local view** rather than separate maps.  
  * Providing **plain-language status text** (“Currently in shadow; Earth just above the southern horizon”) automatically, something QuickMap does not prioritize.

### **4.3 NASA Moon Interactives & Moon Base Learning Resources**

**Intended audience & purpose**

* NASA Moon Interactives and Moon Base Learning Resources offer 3D visualization apps and interactives to “visualize, explore, and analyze the lunar surface” and to bring the lunar south pole and mission environments to life.[**\[75\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/)**[\[77\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20150019680/downloads/20150019680.pdf)[\[92\]](https://moon.nasa.gov/moon-in-motion/interactives/)[\[96\]](https://www.ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150019680)**\[154\]\[157\][**\[190\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/interactive/)**[\[239\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/)[\[342\]](https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/blog/nasa-uses-unreal-engine-to-plan-future-missions)[\[343\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20150019680)**  
* Aimed at educators, students, and the public as part of a curated resource package.[**\[191\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)**[\[220\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/lunar-south-pole-resources/)**\[279\][**\[283\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)

**Strengths**

* 3D exploration of terrain and samples, often with narrative context (e.g., comparing Artemis regions to Apollo sites).  
* Visual simulations of south-pole lighting and “shadows near the Moon’s South Pole” used for outreach and education.[**\[55\]**](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4653)**[\[122\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4650)[\[159\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4486)[\[162\]](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4489)[\[230\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/lunar-south-pole/shadows)[\[231\]](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/shadows-near-the-moons-south-pole/)[\[190\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moonbase/interactive/)**

**Barriers & gaps**

* Many experiences are standalone visualizations or videos with limited user control; others are downloadable applications, which raise installation and hardware barriers.  
* Temporal exploration often limited to pre-rendered animations rather than interactive, arbitrary time selection.

**Opportunities for Stargazer**

* Build on these visual languages but keep the experience browser-native, low-friction, and more parameterizable (arbitrary location/time within constraints).  
* Directly link to these resources from deeper explainer pages to avoid duplicating content.

### **4.4 Other relevant tools and experiences**

* **NASA Eyes** — 3D visualization suite for exploring missions and celestial bodies in the browser; offers compelling camera control and guided tours, used in classrooms.[**\[6\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/lunar_misconceptions/)**[\[43\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/learn/tag/NASA%E2%80%99s%20Eyes)[\[44\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/teach/activity/visualizing-missions-with-nasas-eyes/)[\[291\]](https://eyes.nasa.gov/apps/solar-system/)**  
  * Lesson: robust camera presets and well-scripted tours make 3D navigation approachable.  
* **Infiniscope & digital moon-phase lessons** — evaluated interactive experiences for moon phases and Earth–Moon system, showing digital, inquiry-based designs can improve understanding.[**\[158\]\[293\]**](https://infiniscope.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/)  
  * Lesson: scaffolding sequence (predict → explore → explain) is effective and generalizable to Stargazer’s timeline use.  
* **Serious games and VR lunar exploration experiences** — VR games that immerse players in lunar mission activities have been designed to build interest and motivate learning, with encouraging results for engagement.[**\[62\]**](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**[\[64\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050915009397)[\[80\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-XXXX-X_10)[\[81\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[372\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042815009397)[\[373\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2019.00018)**  
  * Lesson: heavy VR is beyond current scope, but elements like role framing (“You are a mission planner choosing a safe site”) can be borrowed without full gamification.

**5Part 5 — Stargazer Usability and Product Review**

*(Based on the NASA Space Apps Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge brief and Stargazer’s GitHub/description; this section intentionally flags inferred issues as such.)*

### **5.1 Existing relevant features (from project description)**

From the challenge and the Stargazer repository description:[**\[12\]**](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**[\[13\]](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii/)[\[15\]](https://github.com/EAZYCODER2415/stargazer-clps-lunar-navigator)**

* Interactive 3D lunar surface visualization, likely using real elevation data for the south polar region.  
* Ability to show the Sun’s position relative to local horizon over time.  
* Ability to show Earth’s visibility from a landing site.  
* Timeline or controls to vary date/time and see changing illumination and visibility.  
* Comparison between different candidate landing sites.

These map directly onto educationally relevant capabilities identified above.

### **5.2 Potential usability problems**

**Complexity for novices**

* If Stargazer exposes all parameters (date, time, longitude/latitude, camera controls, layers) immediately, novices may confront the same cognitive overload issues documented for Moon Trek and QuickMap.[**\[56\]**](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44322-024-00007-8)**[\[57\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)[\[61\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)[\[288\]](https://www.aspbooks.org/a/volumes/article_details/?paper_id=XXXX)[\[399\]](https://www.goldensoftware.com/communicate-complex-data/)**  
* Time controls can be particularly confusing without clear units and feedback; medical-informatics timeline research shows users struggle when multiple scales and events are shown without clear structure.[**\[329\]\[330\]**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMCXXXXX)**[\[331\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0742051X15000655)**

**Lack of embedded onboarding**

* Visualization-onboarding research suggests novices benefit from guided, in-situ tutorials and example tasks.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[32\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[152\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[153\]\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)** If Stargazer currently relies on external documentation or none at all, teachers and public users may not reach the “aha” moments the tool can provide.

**Jargon and missing plain-language text**

* Without explicit design, labels like “solar elevation,” “azimuth,” or “illumination fraction” will likely appear; science-communication guidelines and plain-language mandates stress that such terms require in-context glossaries and non-technical paraphrases.[**\[34\]**](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-02436-4)**[\[35\]](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1717636115)[\[150\]](https://authorservices.wiley.com/asset/photos/licensing/PLS_guidelines.pdf)[\[151\]](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/)**\[359\]

### **5.3 Missing educational support**

When compared to NASA/LPI educational materials:

* **No explicit curriculum alignment or activity flows.** Existing NASA activities embed goals (“students will be able to…”) and question sequences; Stargazer likely lacks such wrappers yet.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[32\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[33\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-XXXX-X_10)[\[173\]](https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/education-outreach/sample-disks/)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**  
* **No built-in misconception targeting.** LPI and NASA education pages explicitly list common misconceptions as starting points; Stargazer can incorporate this logic (e.g., built-in checks about phases, day/night differences).[**\[17\]\[54\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[89\]](https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2001/ast13dec_1/)[\[296\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[350\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)[\[352\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**  
* **Limited accessibility hints.** There is no current indication of alt text, keyboard navigation, or audio description support, despite guidance from IDATA, NISE Net and accessibility literature for astronomy visualization.[**\[13\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nisenet.org/blind-low-vision)[\[69\]](https://idataproject.org/)[\[314\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.XXXX)[\[325\]](https://accessibility.huit.harvard.edu/data-visualization)**

### **5.4 Features likely too complicated for beginners**

Potentially high-friction capabilities include:

* Arbitrary coordinate entry and unconstrained camera motion.  
* Simultaneous use of many overlays (terrain, illumination maps, communication visibility, etc.), contrary to USWDS recommendations to limit visualizations for non-experts to a small number of concepts per view.[**\[316\]\[327\]**](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualization/)**[\[380\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)**  
* Raw numeric readouts (e.g., degrees, fractions) without qualitative interpretation.

**Implication:** Where such capabilities are necessary to meet challenge specs, they should be *hidden behind an “advanced” toggle* or only surfaced in educator/expert modes.

**7Part 7 — TECHNICAL TEAM HANDOVER**

This section is written as a concise to-do list for developers.

### **7.1 Must-do improvements (P0)**

1. **Implement guided “First Visit” south-pole tour**  
   * **What:** Add an optional tour that automatically sets a south-pole site, steps through a handful of key time points, and explains each step with one-sentence captions.  
   * **Who it benefits:** Both teachers (class demo starter) and public users (first-launch onboarding).  
   * **Why it matters:** Without onboarding, non-expert users get lost; research shows stepwise guidance significantly increases comprehension of complex visualizations.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[152\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**  
   * **Success definition:** In informal testing, most new users who start the tour finish it and can then manipulate time and camera independently.  
2. **Add plain-language scene status panel**  
   * **What:** A small text area that auto-updates based on current site/time, summarizing illumination and Earth visibility in everyday language.  
   * **Who:** Both personas.  
   * **Why:** Connects visuals to conceptual understanding and addresses widespread misconceptions (e.g., Moon illumination).[**\[17\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[25\]](https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21798)[\[258\]](https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/moon-phases/en/)**  
   * **Success:** Users can answer basic “what’s happening now?” questions correctly after glancing at the panel.  
3. **Simplify time interaction with presets**  
   * **What:** Primary timeline limited to a small, visible window around a scenario plus labeled presets (e.g., local sunrise, local “noon”); advanced controls in a separate panel.  
   * **Who:** Both personas; especially important for classroom use.  
   * **Why:** Research shows intuitive, constrained timelines improve interpretability; complex time input is a major usability trap.[**\[161\]**](https://www.timeanddate.com/moon/phases/)**[\[329\]\[330\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMCXXXXX)[\[383\]](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1176041)**  
   * **Success:** Users can quickly explore one full “lunar day” at a site without confusion about what the controls mean.  
4. **Create at least two teacher activity templates**  
   * **What:** Short activity descriptions (objectives, steps, questions) accessible from within Stargazer and exportable.  
   * **Who:** Teachers.  
   * **Why:** Teachers need structured, time-bounded lessons; lack of ready-made activities is a recognized adoption barrier.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[21\]\[39\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)[\[362\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**  
   * **Success:** At least one teacher can run a 30–40 minute class using only the template and the tool.  
5. **Glossary and tooltips for key terms**  
   * **What:** Implement glossary definitions and hover/focus tooltips for terms like “elevation,” “azimuth,” “illumination,” “local lunar day,” etc.  
   * **Who:** Both personas.  
   * **Why:** Plain-language guidance is critical for non-experts; reduces jargon barrier.[**\[34\]**](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-02436-4)**[\[150\]](https://authorservices.wiley.com/asset/photos/licensing/PLS_guidelines.pdf)[\[151\]](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/)[\[316\]](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualization/)[\[337\]](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/azel.html)[\[338\]](https://solardat.uoregon.edu/)**\[359\]  
   * **Success:** Users correctly paraphrase at least some definitions after reading tooltips.  
6. **Clarify limits: power and comms disclaimers**  
   * **What:** Add concise, visible text near relevant UI elements that explicitly states the tool only shows geometric visibility, not power-generation or communications performance.  
   * **Who:** Both; important for any public or educational claims.  
   * **Why:** Prevents misinterpretation and aligns with technical literature distinguishing illumination and actual system design.[**\[261\]\[264\]**](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**[\[268\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/24/5691)[\[269\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[272\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063317302855)[\[305\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**  
   * **Success:** No copy or UI suggests direct equivalence between sunlight and power, or Earth visibility and guaranteed link; disclaimers easy to find.

### **7.2 Recommended improvements (P1)**

1. **Two-site comparison mode**  
   * **What:** Simple toggle between two curated sites with synchronized camera and time, plus prompts/questions in the UI.  
   * **Who:** Teachers and students; also interesting to public.  
   * **Why:** Comparison is central to the challenge brief and to educational activities; existing resources (LabXchange, LPI) show it’s effective.[**\[32\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)**[\[149\]](https://www.labxchange.org/library/)**\[384\]\[386\]  
   * **Success:** Users can articulate at least one meaningful difference between sites after using the mode.  
2. **“Classroom-safe” preset mode**  
   * **What:** A mode that locks to vetted sites, limited time range, and stable camera presets; hides advanced controls.  
   * **Who:** Teachers.  
   * **Why:** Reduces risk of confusion in live demos; addresses teacher concerns around tool complexity.[**\[21\]\[39\]\[362\]**](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**[\[363\]](https://www.edweek.org/technology)**  
   * **Success:** Teachers can operate Stargazer live in a 10–15 minute segment without needing to manage advanced options.  
3. **Baseline accessibility enhancements**  
   * **What:** Ensure keyboard navigation for core controls; add alt text and descriptive captions; adjust color/contrast for overlays.  
   * **Who:** Both, with particular benefit for users with disabilities and classrooms with constrained viewing conditions.  
   * **Why:** Aligns with astronomy accessibility initiatives (NISE Net, IDATA) and general visualization-accessibility guidance.[**\[13\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis-ii/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nisenet.org/blind-low-vision)[\[69\]](https://idataproject.org/)[\[95\]](https://libguides.lib.msu.edu/dataviz)[\[314\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.XXXX)[\[325\]](https://accessibility.huit.harvard.edu/data-visualization)**  
   * **Success:** Basic WCAG compliance for interactions; at least one external accessibility check passes core flows.  
4. **Site “story cards”**  
* **What:** Text snippets for each featured site explaining why it’s important and how it relates to Artemis and resources like ice.  
* **Who:** Public users, students, teachers needing talking points.  
* **Why:** Storytelling and context drive engagement; NASA partners routinely frame sites narratively.[**\[191\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)**[\[195\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)[\[242\]](https://www.nasa.gov/stem/artemis-for-kids.html)[\[245\]](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/resources/artemis.asp)[\[249\]](https://www.elsevier.com/books/space-science-and-public-engagement/)[\[250\]](https://chandra.harvard.edu/edu/)**  
* **Success:** Users recall at least one reason a site is interesting after reading its card.  
1. **Misconception-aware micro-explanations**  
* **What:** Toggleable or hover-triggered texts that explicitly address common lunar misconceptions and guide users to use the tool to test them.  
* **Who:** Both personas.  
* **Why:** Research shows misconceptions are resilient without explicit confrontation and refutation.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[16\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)[\[17\]\[54\]\[296\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[350\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)[\[352\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**  
* **Success:** After interacting with at least one micro-explanation, users show improved accuracy on a small concept check.

### **7.3 Optional future features (P2)**

1. **Challenge prompts and mini-quests**  
* **What:** A few optional in-app challenges (e.g., “Find a time when this site is in shadow but still sees Earth”) with simple completion feedback.  
* **Who:** Public and student users.  
* **Why:** Light gamification boosts engagement without full game complexity; can double as formative assessment.[**\[62\]**](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**[\[372\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042815009397)[\[373\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2019.00018)[\[374\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0742051X15000655)[\[375\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6404/aa7c1f)**  
* **Success:** Observed usage of challenge feature and anecdotal reports of increased engagement.  
1. **Text-only time-series summaries**  
* **What:** Generate textual or CSV summaries of illumination and Earth visibility over a chosen interval (for offline analysis or accessibility).  
* **Who:** Teachers (homework/analysis tasks), accessibility users, advanced hobbyists.  
* **Why:** Builds on patterns from LROC illumination maps but in a simpler, more accessible form; supports accessibility.[**\[140\]**](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/)**[\[160\]\[260\]](http://lroc.sese.asu.edu/illumination)[\[264\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)**  
* **Success:** Example lesson/analysis successfully constructed using exported data; accessible mode users report value.

**8Part 8 — Presentation-Ready Summary**

**Three key teacher findings**

1. Many teachers and even preservice educators hold persistent misconceptions about lunar phases and Earth–Sun–Moon geometry, and they report low confidence with specialized astronomy tools, despite positive attitudes toward digital technology.[**\[16\]**](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)**[\[21\]\[39\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[54\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[350\]](https://www.tused.org/index.php/tused/article/download/101/59/125)[\[362\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)**  
2. Interactive 3D and simulation-based tools, when embedded in structured activities, significantly improve student understanding of spatial astronomy concepts and increase engagement compared to traditional instruction.[**\[3\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[7\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)[\[11\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)[\[41\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131517302810)[\[61\]](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/edu/news/2015/7/28/)[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[73\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.XXXX)[\[158\]](https://infiniscope.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/)**  
3. Teachers adopt tools most readily when they come with curriculum-aligned, time-bounded activities, clear onboarding, and modest interface complexity — exactly the combination NASA and LPI provide in their most-used lunar education resources.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[19\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814002043)[\[47\]](https://trek.nasa.gov/education/)[\[173\]](https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/education-outreach/sample-disks/)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**

**Three key public findings**

1. Public interest in lunar exploration is high and emotionally positive, especially around Artemis; people are eager for experiences that let them “be there” and understand what makes specific polar sites special.[**\[12\]**](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)**[\[14\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2021.XXXXX)[\[21\]](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/10.1080/XXXX)[\[87\]\[90\]](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/americans-express-pride-us-space-program)[\[191\]](https://science.nasa.gov/moon/earths-moon-resources/)[\[195\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/)**  
2. Non-specialists struggle with abstract astronomical concepts (phases, illumination, Earth-from-Moon perspective) and are easily overwhelmed by expert tools that present many layers and controls without guidance.[**\[4\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)**[\[6\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/lunar_misconceptions/)[\[17\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)[\[70\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/misconceptions/)[\[88\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)[\[94\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-01606-5_1)[\[399\]](https://www.goldensoftware.com/communicate-complex-data/)**  
3. Interactive, story-driven exhibits and digital experiences — especially those with simple interactions, narrative framing, and layered explanations — are effective at capturing attention and fostering meaningful engagement in museums, planetariums and online.[**\[14\]**](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2021.XXXXX)**[\[23\]](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.XXXXX)[\[51\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272775718300143)[\[52\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042814031239)**\[124\]\[125\][**\[361\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S187704281500673X)

**Three strongest product recommendations**

1. **Build a guided, layered “First Visit” experience and plain-language status panel as the default entry path.** This addresses the biggest UX barrier (initial confusion) and directly supports conceptual understanding for both teachers and the public.[**\[31\]**](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**[\[72\]](https://aas.org/education/wwt-ambassadors)[\[88\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1574013725000085)[\[150\]](https://authorservices.wiley.com/asset/photos/licensing/PLS_guidelines.pdf)[\[151\]](https://www.plainlanguage.gov/)[\[382\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3359996.3364700)**  
2. **Provide teacher-focused scaffolding: classroom-safe presets, activity templates, and two-site comparison mode.** These changes convert Stargazer from a demo into a usable classroom tool aligned with existing NASA/LPI practice.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[4\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/resources/s_system/moon.shtml)[\[32\]](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290605.3300916)[\[33\]](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-XXXX-X_10)[\[173\]](https://ares.jsc.nasa.gov/education-outreach/sample-disks/)[\[348\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/)[\[349\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/explore/lunar_south_pole/background/)**  
3. **Design for cognitive and conceptual accessibility: glossary tooltips, misconception-aware explanations, constrained overlays, and visible disclaimers about power and communications.** This protects scientific integrity and maximizes learning impact for non-expert audiences.[**\[17\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**[\[25\]](https://www.nap.edu/catalog/21798)[\[261\]\[264\]](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/XXXX)[\[316\]\[327\]](https://designsystem.digital.gov/components/data-visualization/)[\[352\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/education/pre_service_edu/PhasesMisconceptions.shtml)**\[359\]

**One-sentence value statement for Stargazer**

Stargazer can become an intuitive, story-rich lunar landing-site explorer that turns authentic NASA south-pole data into classroom-ready lessons and engaging public experiences, helping non-experts *see* and *understand* how sunlight, shadows, and Earth visibility shape the challenges of exploring and living on the Moon.
